speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to say a few words on Bill C-135 presently before us and entitled "An Act to provide additional financing mechanisms and institutions for the residential mortgage market in Canada".
Mr. Speaker, I shall state right away that, as far as I am concerned, properties are quite mortgaged enough just now.
I think that this bill, which aims at increasing mortgages on the properties of Canadians, thereby dispossessing them through a legislation of Parliament, is going somewhat too far. This will be another institution which will enable some financiers to make tax free investments and capital gains. I believe that the purpose of this bill is to increase the opportunities for certain institutions and certain financiers.
I agree with those who say that we have quite enough of this kind of institutions in Canada. If the government were to submit, for example, a bill to abolish the 11 per cent tax on building materials, I would say that we were making progress, that we were accomplishing something, that we were moving ahead, because we would be giving the people means they do not have today, advantages that they would need and which they do not have.
This bill will not lower the interest rates; this bill will not make it possible for more citizens to become property owners. This bill will deprive many people of the right to own property, and it is the government which, in the final analysis, will be the guarantor of these mortgages. When the government sticks its nose into private business, it takes over, and private businesses disappear, private initiative disappears. I believe that we have reached quite a point in this respect, and that the government has already stick its nose too far into private enterprise.
Private enterprise, which should be sacred above all else, is not a monopoly, but government enterprise is. It is for this reason that we should stand firm against the intrusion by government into private business, for in so doing it takes away the rights and prerogatives of citizens
June 12, 1973

to make something of themselves, it deprives them of their right to make their way in society, it dampens their initiative, and through these various methods of control, increasingly dispossesses private enterprise.
I therefore ask the hon. minister what more this type of mortgage loan company will do to give citizens the opportunity to obtain their very o\yn homes. As a matter of fact, 97 per cent of the homes being bought at this time, Mr. Speaker, are acquired through the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. With new types of mortgages granted by mortgage investment companies, we want to reach a 100 per cent mark.
Will taxpayers receive more assistance from these mortgage investment companies than they are getting now? Will the housing problem be solved this way? Is it a way of solving the housing problem? The problem will not be solved anymore than it is today. We will have more trouble than at present, and taxpayers will not have any other alternative but to go deeper into debt, to mortgage themselves, to increase their private debts while increasing the public debt. There is no other solution with the kind of governments we have now. No other solution can be presented to the Canadian people. They do not find any and when some people advocate solutions, they find that funny and they laugh.
How magnificent, Mr. Speaker, the economic conditions today! How magnificent the federal, provincial and municipal government deficits, not to mention deficits as well! How magnificent the $125 to $130 billion debts of all governments and of all Canadians bearing interest at 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 20 or 24 per cent! What a splendid kind of administration!
That is what they wish to keep on offering the people; that is what they call reforms. Mr. Speaker, they are shameful reforms that should never have seen the light in this country, because human beings will be more and more dispossessed, while they should on the contrary get the upper hand. Power, Mr. Speaker, should be in the hands of the citizens, not in the hands of a usurping state that has no respect for citizens.
Mr. Speaker, there is one problem to solve, namely the housing problem. To solve it, the minister should have introduced a bill by saying: Beginning today, those who will provide mortgage loans on houses or property will not get more than a 3 per cent interest. Mr. Speaker, property is as important as bread and butter, because citizens must live in houses, because that is a part of the family life and of the life of the individual.
The great house of our Lord, Mr. Speaker, is beautiful, it is great, it is good, but houses must be built by citizens in this country, and those houses must be the property of those citizens. Now they want to give that to the state because citizens, according to the government, according to the minister, are not intelligent enough to build houses for themselves and pay for them.
The current system denies any intelligence to our fellow citizens. When an 11 per cent tax is charged on building materials, when houses are mortgaged for 25, 30 or 40 years, when owners have to pay a house seven or eight times over, this is called progress, this is called sound administration and a just society. It is a just society for
Mortgage Financing Bill
the richest taxpayers and their friends but "just" for them. But it is not just for the people. It is injustice for most of them.
And it is justice that should prevail. We are here to speak about justice and not simply to adopt laws dispossessing everyone. We have had in the past too many of those restrictive laws and this will have to end some day or else we shall have what other countries have had: revolution. This is what we shall have and we know it.
But nobody cares; it is much preferred to protect the money capital rather than the human capital. The money capital is all-important whereas the human capital does not matter. The human capital is forgotten and replaced by the money capital. This is where we failed and where we do not take our responsibilities. We shall take our responsibilities when the human capital is given first priority and when the laws are used to meet people's needs and allow them to enjoy their country instead of giving it up to two, three or four big businessmen who have taken over the laws and have made a valet out of the government.
The government is no longer the master of the situation it has become a valet and this must not be allowed to last. This is why power should be regained by the government provided it is loyal and social spirit prevails rather than a spirit of bestiality and exploitation.
We would have much to say on this point, but we want to defend especially the private sector. As a matter of fact, we are its defender because it is thanks to private enterprise and not only to public enterprise that we will develop a strong country.
The state should have control only over big things, only over large and important institutions which are too expensive or too big for private enterprise. And the government should protect private enterprise in all its efforts by reducing interest rates, removing taxes on building materials, giving the citizens the right and the ability to pay a house within at least ten years.
It is not logical that our legislation prevent Canadians from having something of their own, especially suitable housing. They get a mortgage for 20, 30 or 40 years. And it seems normal to have a mortgage on life. This is not normal and if a Canadian pays too many taxes and is unable to purchase a house within ten years, it is not logical to mortgage him for 40 years. And after 40 years, this house will have to be re-built. Their heirs will not be able to use these old houses; new ones will have to be built while the old ones will not even be paid for.
Therefore, what should be done to protect private enterprise? That is a question I ask the minister. I ask him as well what gave him the idea of establishing that kind of mortgage investment companies and what he intends to protect. I ask him to be frank, to tell us who is going to take advantage of these mortgages. Should these mortgages not be left to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and to other existing institutions?
Since a few banks are allowed at present to make loans on mortgages, let us help them. This government has no right to interfere with this, and it will have to stop doing

June 12, 1973
Mortgage Financing Bill
it; private interprise will then exist. There is no need for us to set up new mortgage loans companies as we have all that is required.
The minister was saying that there exists in Canada four important institutions which are authorized to make loans on mortgages. Such a situation will not be corrected by setting up a fifth one because people or capitalists lending money nowadays are doing it with big publicity.
The caisses populaires are overflowing with credit and urging people to build houses; they are ready to finance them. Then, we do not need that new mortgage corporation which would be just like the others. Mr. Speaker, that corporation will need other taxpayers, will hire more civil servants and will incur new expenses. It may become another department which will eat up more taxes to pay the civil servants salaries when we already have everything without needing to spend any more money without investing more capital, without hiring more civil servants at high salaries paid with taxpayers taxes to operate a new mortgage corporation.
Mr. Speaker, that corporation is nothing new, it is as old as the hills. It should never have existed. It exists, but that does not mean it is a good thing, for if Canadians are all "mortgaged" it is because of this kind of mortgage corporation.
If today we are all in debt and if we can no longer manage without deficit, Mr. Speaker, it means that something is not working. Once all taxes are paid and taking into account the rising cost of living which also increases government revenues by the billions, Mr. Speaker, the taxpayer will be told that taxes are not being increased. "The taxpayer is protected". That is what they say, Mr. Speaker, and the cost of living is skyrocketing. When the cost of living rises so much, government revenues increase correspondingly.
When a product sells for $100, Mr. Speaker, the federal government gets $12 through his 12 p. 100 tax. If the price of that product rises to $200, government revenues amount to $24 instead of $12. The government therefore makes twice as much money, thanks to the increase in the cost of living. To my mind, that is one of the reasons that explains why the old parties do not want to keep the cost of living from going up. As times goes by, Mr. Speaker, the deeper the citizens sink into debt, the higher the cost of living goes and the more difficult it becomes to make ends meet.
Are we here to compound the problems, or are we here to ease the burden inflicted upon the citizens by taxes of all sorts, of which the new taxes levied to make up the government deficits, federal, provincial, municipal as well as educational? All of them have deficits. Canadians can no longer meet their needs. The government is asked to help at every turn: subsidies for this, subsidies for that, because the citizens have been stripped of their money.
A way must be found, Mr. Speaker, of returning this power to the citizens. The money should belong to the citizens; it should be in their hands. These mortgage loan companies will act as the government now does: they will sell bonds, they will seek out all the people's savings, and when private institutions can no longer find anything they will be obliged to appeal to the government. That is what the old parties want, that is what the socialists want,

that the people should all come running to the government for a living that they submit, that they give up everything they hold dear, even down to their freedom.
In this regard I will say to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) that he would be better advised to withdraw his bill, since, in my opinion, it is unacceptable. It seems to me that it is not appropriate under the present circumstances, for there are so many other institutions, Mr. Speaker, capable of doing the job, and savings bonds must remain in the taxpayers' hands as much as possible, instead of remaining in the hands of the government, which corners all the wealth by means of selling bonds.

speechtext:
During the last several days we have listened during the question period to what I would call a debate on increasing interest rates. We who sit here know
June 12, 1973

that if the regular bank rate goes up a half of 1 per cent this will be reflected in increased interest rates for housing.
The people who really need housing today, and for whom I have the greatest sympathy, are the younger couples who are raising families. They are like the child who walks past a candy store; he sees the candy in the store, presses his face against the window pane and thinks how nice it would be if he could have the candy. It is the same with the people who need housing. They think of it with longing, but it is beyond their reach. They do not have the several thousand dollars needed for a down payment on their own shelter. This is the problem that the bill does not tackle. There is not much use thinking that the bill will deal with that situation simply by leaving it to the profit motive to solve the problem. It will not. If we want to use the profit motive we will have to control interest rates and see they are not above a certain level. If we want to solve the problem by what has been referred to as the private enterprise method, then we will have to control land development, which will mean that land developers cannot charge over a certain amount. But these are the things we do not do.
Not long ago the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Harney) put on the record of this House the fact that a group of developers in the Toronto area control all the land for development in the area. One of my colleagues says that most of them are Tories. This group can decide how much rake-off they want from development in the area and whoever wants housing there will pay the price. We are all aware of these facts. Anyone who reads, anyone who looks, anyone who studies must 1 aware of these facts. I know that in the city of Saskatoon students have told me that certain low cost developments in that city are closed to them. I have received letters from churches that were trying to provide senior citizens' homes in the city of Saskatoon. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, I think we have a good record in the city of Saskatoon. In many cases we have provided adequate housing for the citizens, but now we face the problem of having to pay interest rates and development costs which make the provision of senior housing very expensive.
Bill C-133 which we passed this afternoon dealt with that problem to some extent. But we must move past that to an over-all approach. The bill which we are now debating fails utterly to reduce to a minimum the cost of mortgage financing for housing. Perhaps we should develop one or two new approaches to housing in Canada. We have a mobile population, composed in the main of younger families. As they advance from one job to another they move freely from one part of Canada to another. We should develop some type of housing that will meet their needs. I do not think we should expect them to have to buy and sell their house every time they move.
Maybe we should consider the provision of rental housing at rents that would be decided on the basis of taxes and interest rates, housing not primarily for low-income people but for people with ordinary incomes so that each time they moved they would not be put to the expense of paying real estate fees and lawyers' fees for the transfer of houses, all of which add to the cost of housing and to inflation.

Mr. Speaker, we should also be thinking of means of ensuring that the cost of shelter will not become prohibitive. We should have comfortable homes for all our citizens. This should be possible in our society without the people who live in such homes being the victims of speculators.
We should not permit high interest rates, high rents and these types of charges which are visited on that part of our population least able to protect itself. subtopic: FINANCE-SUGGESTED STUDY OF MODIFICATION OF BRANCH BANKING SYSTEM TO EASE BURDEN OF HIGH INTEREST RATES ON SLOW GROWTH AREAS
FINANCE-SUGGESTED STUDY OF MODIFICATION OF BRANCH BANKING SYSTEM TO EASE BURDEN OF HIGH INTEREST RATES ON SLOW GROWTH AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 12 I put the following question to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner):
With the minister consider instituting a study of modifications of the branch banking system designed to ease the burden of universal high interest rates on areas of slow economic growth?
The minister's answer was not responsive to the intent of my question, but on April 19 he was kind enough to send me further information. The information is helpful and I appreciate it, but I did want to see a study convened so that we would have an opportunity to make some suggestions. Tonigh.t I shall make some of those suggestions. I trust they will clarify the intent of my question and identify some problem areas, and I hope the minister will find them as constructive as they are intended to be.

We should develop regional banking policies and restructure the branch banking system to provide, among other things, Bank of Canada offices in different regions of Canada, to secure more policy input through different interests. Banks, although formidable institutions, are subject to government policy and are readily influenced by the Bank of Canada. Regional banking policies should be feasible when tight money is in vogue, to protect the interests of slow-growth regions. I believe the so-called Winnipeg agreement tacitly recognizes this need. Due to the nature of our economy, our population dispersement and seasonal employment problems with slow-growth areas, regional answers to monetary problems must be sought.
As long as we have one central bank, one common currency and the branch banking system in Canada all regions are influenced by national monetary conditions, including interest rate levels and the availability of credit. The executive vice-president of the Bank of Nova Scotia, speaking at the Canadian Club, Winnipeg, on April 5 of this year, had this to say:
Clearly, if the chartered banks were permitted to include provincial treasury bills or similar securities in their statutory or even conventional liquid assets, a prerequisite would be that the central bank itself would have to own and deal in the same classes of provincial securities.
He further said:
Likewise, the chartered banks could be permitted to include provincial treasury bills in their statutory secondary reserves, and short-term provincial bonds in their major liquid asset calculation. The market for provincial debt issues would be much improved and the over-all borrowing rate of the provinces would fall, while the federal government's debt servicing costs would probably rise. A side benefit would be that the federal government's issue of treasury bills would become meaningful, which is not the case when about 95 per cent of the treasury bills are held by the Bank of Canada and the chartered banks, as at present.
It is always possible to pose difficulties in the way of new structural arrangements, but I believe that the changes suggested above are feasible and would materially improve the financial markets of the provinces. And that is something more than is likely to emerge from the generalizations in the Speech from the Throne.
It is to me a matter of settled national policy that the government will depress the economy and create unemployment in order to contain inflation. The province of New Brunswick, being a part of Canada, cannot escape the consequences of national policy. When the federal government wants to depress the economy, when it wants to trade off unemployment to contain inflation the economy of New Brunswick suffers, unemployment in New Brunswick increases and we get inflation in the bargain.
The grim fact of life is that those of us who live in the less prosperous regions of Canada are the first to be hit, the hardest hit and the last to recover from such a lag in national economic performance. I am unhappy with the fact that so many people in New Brunswick continued to suffer poverty and unemployment last year, a year in which there was an increase in the labour force itself and in which federal policy persisted in restricting economic expansion.
New Brunswick has no reason to feel gratitude that its ocean ports have been neglected, its transportation serv-
June 12, 1973

ices have deteriorated, its markets lost through national tariff policy and its trade diminished by years of economic centralization. We are not satisfied to see hundreds of millions of dollars spent in developing airports in central Canada while our own regional transportation facilities are losing the ability to handle freight and other services. We are not satisfied that the rail rates imposed by our own railways and sanctioned by the federal transport authority are two to three times as great as those prevailing in competing areas such as the state of Maine. We are not satisfied that when monetary demands in central Canada require the imposition of tight money under an antiquated economic doctrine, the same castor oil treatment is accorded slow-growth areas where the need does not exist.
It is time this government sought modern remedies to modern-day problems. I asked the Minister of Finance to consider a study of this problem. He did not answer the question. The day will come when he will answer, if not to me, to the people.

speakeroldname: Mr. J.-Roland Comtois (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: FINANCE-SUGGESTED STUDY OF MODIFICATION OF BRANCH BANKING SYSTEM TO EASE BURDEN OF HIGH INTEREST RATES ON SLOW GROWTH AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can hardly add anything further to the reply given by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) in answer to the question asked by my hon. colleague.
Indeed, the bank credit expansion rate continues to be very high, and one can hardly expect the government to move towards a restrictive monetary policy. The monetary policy continues to be expansionist, and the credit supply meets the real needs of the economy. Moreover, the Minister of Finance has made a firm commitment to maintain an adequate rate of expansion of the money in circulation, that is, a rate compatible with strong and sustained growth in the production and employment sectors. From this viewpoint, the recent increases in interest rates have been a necessary response to the marked increase in foreign interest rates. Moreover, the heavy demand for credit resulting from a very rapid economic growth has, of course, exerted pressures on interest rates. We may note, however, that short-term rates of interest in Canada fell, early in the year, to much lower levels than comparable rates abroad, and that the Canadian rates are still low when compared with those abroad. It is therefore incorrect to suggest that the recent hike in interest rates reflects a move towards a restrictive monetary policy.
The monetary policy as reflected in the growth of the total amount of money in circulation and in credit conditions in general, is intended to contain any excessive increase in bank credit. The rate of expansion of this bank credit is still high. Bank loans in general have gone up by more than 20 per cent over the twelve-month period ending in May of this year. Since January, these loans have increased at a real rate of approximately 35 per cent. Consumer loans have increased somewhat more rapidly than loans to enterprises, but it is still true that, whatever measure is passed, the expansion of bank credit has been very strong.
It is clear that this very rapid expansion of bank loans must be adjusted downward, at a bearable rate. In Canada as in other countries, slowing down the rate of increase in bank credit sometimes tends to affect more particularly the small enterprises or the less favoured regions of a
Adjournment Debate
country. Now, as the Minister of Finance noted in his answer to my hon. colleague, measures have been adopted to ensure that this adjustment does not lay an undue burden on unfavoured regions or small enterprises in general.
Indeed, the minister and the Governor of the Bank of Canada asked chartered banks to pay particular attention to the needs of small enterprises and poorer regions, and the minister has declared himself satisfied with the favourable reaction of the banks. The Governor of the Bank of Canada is in close communication with chartered banks concerning their practice in granting loans, and the situation is being controlled each day. For the time being, the government is convinced that the chartered banks are doing everything possible to ensure an adequate money supply in those sectors.
In closing my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I will say that it is clearly in the interest of Canadians of all areas of the country to avoid an excessive credit increase. An expansion of credit beyond what is necessary to sustain a strong economic growth would contribute to the inflationary pressures and risk to end in a situation where everyone would be a loser.

subtopic: ENERGY-CAPABILITY OF ENERGY BOARD TO JUDGE APPLICATION TO TRANSPORT NATURAL GAS IN OTHER THAN VAPOUR FORM
ENERGY-CAPABILITY OF ENERGY BOARD TO JUDGE APPLICATION TO TRANSPORT NATURAL GAS IN OTHER THAN VAPOUR FORM
speechtext:
June 12, 1973
Adjournment Debate
A second related question that I should like to put to the minister is: Where will the National Energy Board acquire the competence to make the kind of judgments which, in essence, have more to do with the national economy and with the environment in the sense of ecological values than it has to do with energy? Will the studies into the rail line, the liquid natural gas line, the effects on the economy and on the ecology that are now being undertaken by interdepartmental task forces, so I am informed in answer to order paper questions, be made available to the National Energy Board for study in advance of undertaking any hearing of an application for a gas pipeline? If such information is supplied to the National Energy Board by the government, will the National Energy Board take official notice of the information obtained from such studies and cite it as evidence in support of its conclusions?
A third related question is this: If, indeed, such information is to be made available to the National Energy Board by the government, without which I fail to see how the Energy Board can be considered to have the competence to make the kind of decision the minister attributes to it, then will the information also be made available to parliament so that the elected representatives of the people of Canada will be able to pass judgment upon the decision of the National Energy Board, which in the final analysis is responsible to parliament?
My final remark is more in the way of a statement of conviction than a question. Even if we are assured that all the information and all the powers, which my questions of this evening have implied are necessary in order for the National Energy Board to make a competent decision with respect to a northern pipeline, are placed at the board's disposal, I would deny that it is right and proper that a non-elective body such as the National Energy Board, rather than parliament, should make a decision of such magnitude.
Just listen, Mr. Speaker, to what the draft report on the Evaluation of the Impact on the National Economy of a Northern Canadian Gas Pipe Line says about the economic effect of the demand for $4.5 to $5 billion of capital. At page 13 the report reads:
The construction and operation of a northern gas pipeline, even if it were to carry a substantial proportion of Canadian gas, would likely prove to be a mixed blessing to Canada.
On the following page the report reads:
During pipeline operations, the maximum benefits to Canada would be additional Canadian incomes of $366 million per year, of which government revenues would comprise $73 million, and 150 to 200 permanent jobs.
The potential costs of pipeline operations include:
(a)	a continuous upward pressure of up to $183 million per year
on the Canadian dollar, making it more difficult for other, more
labour-intensive, exports to be sold abroad; and
(b)	a potentially serious upward pressure on the level of the
Canadian energy prices.
I am not willing to have an appointed board make a decision involving implications of that magnitude. I would insist that that is a job for the representatives of the people, for the Parliament of Canada. If I may, in the few seconds remaining to me, be permitted an aside, I find it passing strange, if indeed the economic effects that I have

just put on the record do result from a huge demand for capital for the construction of a vapour state gas pipeline, that the government is not doing something to reduce the costs involved in constructing such a line. For example, I find it difficult to understand why the government feels it is not necessary to finance a test loop for a liquid natural gas pipeline in order to discover whether the potential saving of up to 50 per cent claimed for such a system is indeed realizable.
Instead of doing that, the government has said that is the responsibility of the industry. Private industry is not interested in doing that because right now gas has a seller's market and the constructing of test loops would mean a delay. Customers will absorb the additional costs in any case. If there is a saving to be made, it must first come from government action.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: ENERGY-CAPABILITY OF ENERGY BOARD TO JUDGE APPLICATION TO TRANSPORT NATURAL GAS IN OTHER THAN VAPOUR FORM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has made clear what he had in mind in his rather shotgun question of several days ago. May I just deal with his last point first, which, with all respect, I suggest is absurd. I refer to the suggestion that private industry, if it found it infinitely cheaper to ship natural gas in liquid state rather than in vapour state, would not do so. Obviously, if a pipeline could be made more economic by shipping natural gas in that way, then no doubt it would be done.
The hon. gentleman has expressed indignation at the fact that parliament will not consider this matter. He seems to be ignorant of the fact that the process followed by parliament in respect of pipelining is ordination by parliament. Parliament decided after the experience of pipeline applications in the 1950s and after the Borden commission to specifically pass a law by which these applications would go before a fully qualified and independent economic tribunal, namely, the National Energy Board, for consideration and, if approved by the board, would go on to the governor in council for approval or rejection at that point, or for judgment at the political level.
For the last several years we have made available to the House, to the hon. member and his colleagues, a great deal of information with regard to the possibilities of a northern pipeline. We now have a reference before the committee. In spite of this, it is strange that there has not been the slightest interest on the part of the hon. member and his colleagues elsewhere. If he is so interested in having parliament discuss pipelining, why have he and his colleagues not gone to work on this committee? I personally would be glad to discuss this very interesting issue with them as I have been discussing it.
The hon. member says the board has no competence in economics and ecology. Where has he been for the last 12 years? I suspect he has not read a single decision of the Energy Board. The economics of pipelining and the physical problems created for the environment by the construction of a pipeline have been the very essence of the business of the National Energy Board for the last 12 years.
I go back to my statement which was unequivocal. I said the board has competence and has exercised that competence for the last 12 years under the direction of parlia-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 28 I raised in the House of Commons the case of Tara Singh Gill of India. I urged the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) to rule this man become eligible for landed immigrant status. A principle of justice is at stake here and that is why I will pursue this matter until justice is obtained.
It is impossible to adequately summarize this case in the time available to me, but here are the main points. Mr. Gill, a 26-year old technical school graduate from Punjab, is one of the thousands of visitors who came to Canada from many countries on tourist visas. Under the 1967 Canada Immigration Act, visitors had the right to apply for landed immigrant status from within Canada until that right was suddenly withdrawn by the government on November 3, 1972.
The Minister of Manpower and Immigration told the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration on April 5 that certain cases of individuals in the country before November 3 would be reviewed to determine if landed immigrant status could be granted. He said:
We will also look favourably at cases of persons where there is acceptable evidence that they had called at an immigration office on or before the day of the announcement, but were unable to be dealt with for one reason or another.
At the hearing conducted by the special inquiry officer in Edmonton, a statutory declaration was entered in evidence, signed by Maghar S. Dhaliwal, which reads in paragraph 4:
That on the third day of November 1972, at approximately 4.20 p.m., I, on behalf of Tara Singh Gill, telephoned the immigration office in Edmonton and spoke with Mr. Hampton for the purpose of arranging an appointment for Tara Singh Gill, who wished to apply for immigrant status in Canada.
Mr. Dhaliwal was told that since time was running short for the day, Mr. Gill should come to the immigration office on Monday, November 6. He was there at 8.30 a.m. the following Monday. He was refused application forms for landed immigrant status, whereupon he received immigration form 1010 so that his brother Gurdial Singh Gill could nominate him for landed immigrant status.
Adjournment Debate
In his review of the evidence the minister has drawn the conclusion that it was only on March 20, 1973, that Tara Singh Gill indicated his desire to become a landed immigrant. From the confused presentation at several hearings I can understand how the minister might have drawn this conclusion, but I ask him to deepen his review of this case. Tara Singh Gill arrived in Canada on October 26. He was in the midst of looking around to determine his future, as he was permitted to by law, when lightning struck in the form of the government announcement. There followed the quick action by Mr. Dhaliwal, on Mr. Gill's behalf, on November 3. On November 10, Mr. Empson, the district administrator, acknowledged Mr. Gill's desire for permanent residence.
On January 9, Mr. Gill was admitted to Grant MacEwan Community College in Edmonton to take a course as a biomedical equipment technician. How, then, can there be any doubt that Tara Singh Gill wanted to stay in Canada? On what ground is Mr. Dhaliwal's statutory declaration doubted? Mr. Dhaliwal is a Canadian citizen and an officer with the federal Department of Agriculture in Edmonton, and there is nothing to put his credibility in question.
I do not doubt the minister's sincerity when he speaks of acceptable evidence of an attempt being made to start landed immigrant proceedings on or before November 3. What has happened is that Tara Singh Gill has been caught in a maze of bureaucracy. He has been ordered deported. He has appealed the deportation order, and to make matters worse he has been refused a work permit by the Department of Manpower and Immigration while this appeal is pending. He does not want to be dependent upon his brother. He has been offered a job with Vanguard Concrete Products, and I verified today that the job is still open to him. But he is being discriminated against. He has been abused by the bureaucracy and denied a chance to work. This is not the spirit of the Canada of which we are proud. An injustice has been committed against a young man who shows every sign of being a good Canadian citizen if we give him the chance.
Mr. Speaker, I want to make it clear to the minister that I support the step taken to prohibit applications for landed immigrant status from within Canada. Whatever the merits of the 1967 law, this section became open to abuse. But the law should not have been changed retroactively. I protest the retroactivity and I challenge its moral correctness, whatever the legal niceties. Even with retroactivity, the minister opened the door to people like Tara Singh Gill, but then his officials shut it.
Mr. Speaker, I see opposite me the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. MacGuigan). I want to say to him that I hope he will not give me a "canned" answer prepared by the department. The personal reputation for integrity and justice of the parliamentary secretary is well known in this country and he is greatly respected by me. I want him to be able to study this case in the detail I have before he gives a definitive answer, especially an answer in the negative.
I say, for the sake of justice, for Canada's good name, for a true welcome to India's Prime Minister, Madam Gandhi, who will grace this chamber with her presence in a few days, open the door to Tara Singh Gill.

June 12, 1973

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that when this case was originally raised by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche) the person concerned had not at that time been ordered deported. Since then an immigration inquiry has been held and Mr. Gill's deportation ordered. Since an appeal has been lodged with the Immigration Appeal Board against that order, it would be inappropriate to discuss the merits of the case at this time. Now that this matter is before the board, it alone has the responsibility for assessing, not only the legality of the order made at the inquiry but also whether there are compassionate or humanitarian considerations on which the order should be set aside.
When the decision was taken to remove the right of visitors to apply to remain permanently, it was not intended that wholesale exemptions would be made to this policy. I emphasize the word "visitors". The previous provision which allowed a person to adjust his status was not established as an alternate method of immigrating to the traditional and accepted procedure of applying abroad.
Obviously, the minister cannot nor would he wish to review the decisions of staff in every case. I can assure the House, however, that all immigration field staff in Canada know of the minister's desire for a compassionate approach to problems of this kind. Indeed, as an indication of the field staff's approach, there have been many recommendations to the minister for exemption from the revocation of regulation 34 on compassionate grounds. Although I do not have any statistics immediately available, literally hundreds of these requests have gone forward for governor in council approval in the six months since the revocation of regulation 34. Those who like Mr. Gill are not satisfied with the decision of the department have recourse to the full process of the law through the special inquiry and appeal procedures. Mr. Gill has taken advantage of this process.
One matter which the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona mentioned and which concerns me is the denial of the right to an employment visa to Mr. Gill. On the basis of further facts which might be presented by the hon. member, I know the minister would wish to review this very important question to be sure that either justice has been done already to Mr. Gill or that an employment visa should be granted to him.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10.28 p.m.

Wednesday, June 13, 1973
